module_title: Elastic Load Balancing, Routing and Target Health
review_basis: Individually visually inspected original SAP Module 08 slides 16–18.
part_title: PrivateLink, NLB-to-ALB and GWLB Stateful Inspection

scenes.title: PrivateLink and NLB-to-ALB service composition
scenes.visual_overview: The upper panels show a PrivateLink endpoint service backed by NLB and consumers through interface endpoints. The lower panels show NLB forwarding to ALB with matching TCP port and health checks.
visual_walkthrough: Trace endpoint service publication with NLB, allowed principals and optional acceptance
Clarify that PrivateLink offers narrow service connectivity rather than full VPC network peering
Follow NLB-to-ALB target composition for static IP or PrivateLink with ALB HTTP routing
Verify NLB and ALB same VPC/account constraints, TCP target group matching the ALB listener port and health checks
scenes.visual_example: A partner exposes one private web API across accounts through PrivateLink, with an NLB carrying connections to an ALB that routes HTTP requests by path.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Compose NLB and ALB only when static entry or PrivateLink plus HTTP routing justifies extra cost and failure points.
scenes.narration: This slide explains two related but distinct service boundaries. In the upper-left, a provider publishes an endpoint service backed by an NLB. Consumers connect to that service through interface endpoints, with provider allowed-principal permissions and acceptance requirements as configured. Follow the dotted arrows to the consumer endpoints. The second panel makes an important restriction explicit: PrivateLink exposes a specified service and does not create broad VPC peering. Provider networking, consumer endpoint security and identity authorization still matter. In the lower-left, the architecture combines two load balancers. An NLB can forward to an ALB target, allowing the NLB's static addresses or PrivateLink service access to coexist with the ALB's HTTP host and path routing. Trace first through the NLB, then through the ALB to the application targets. The lower-right requirements are operationally important: the NLB and ALB must be in the same VPC and account for this supported integration. Use a TCP target group targeting the ALB on a port that matches an ALB listener, and configure health checks. Consider whether the extra component, cost and troubleshooting surface are actually justified.

scenes.title: Gateway Load Balancer inserts transparent appliance inspection
scenes.visual_overview: Four panels contrast GWLB Layer 3 transparent appliance distribution, GENEVE UDP 6081 encapsulation, GWLB endpoints across consumer/provider VPCs, and deliberate route steering.
visual_walkthrough: Trace Layer 3 IP traffic to the GWLB inspection service and appliance targets
Explain compatible firewalls or IDS/IPS receiving GENEVE-encapsulated traffic on UDP 6081
Follow traffic from consumer GWLB endpoint to the provider VPC GWLB and appliance fleet
Inspect both forward and return route tables; placing an endpoint alone does not inspect traffic
scenes.visual_example: A central security VPC offers a firewall service to application VPCs through Gateway Load Balancer endpoints and explicit workload subnet routes.
scenes.visual_synthesis: GWLB distributes traffic among appliances; inspection decisions belong to the appliances and the routes must traverse them.
scenes.narration: This is a network-appliance insertion design rather than a standard web load balancer. Start at the upper-left where IP packets enter Gateway Load Balancer. GWLB combines transparent gateway behavior with distribution across compatible firewall, intrusion-detection or intrusion-prevention appliances. Move right to the transport diagram. GWLB encapsulates the original traffic using GENEVE over UDP port six zero eight one, letting the appliance inspect the contained packets while GWLB manages flow distribution. Supported appliance targets can be instances or eligible private IP addresses. Now follow the lower-left section. A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint in a consumer VPC provides a service connection to the GWLB and appliance fleet in the provider VPC. That endpoint is the network insertion point, but it does not automatically capture all traffic in the consumer VPC. The lower-right routing panel is therefore decisive. The appropriate subnet and gateway route tables must steer intended flows through the endpoint and appliance path, including the return journey. A valid appliance security policy is ineffective if traffic can bypass it. GWLB distributes inspection flows; the appliance applies the actual security decision.

scenes.title: GWLB flow affinity and stateful inspection symmetry
scenes.visual_overview: The diagram emphasizes consistent blue request and orange return paths around one stateful inspection appliance, with lower panels about failure reassignment and health evidence.
visual_walkthrough: Examine default five-tuple affinity and when supported three- or two-tuple stickiness applies
Trace both forward and return traffic through the stateful appliance and appliance mode where necessary
Explain health checks, existing-session reassignment and loss of state on a replacement appliance
Review appliance capacity, draining, resilience and real-world flow tests
scenes.visual_example: A central inspection service preserves both directions of a long-lived TCP flow on the same firewall appliance; failover may require application reconnection.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Healthy replacement capacity does not automatically preserve a stateful inspection session or ensure symmetric routing.
scenes.narration: The central shield illustrates a stateful firewall's dependency on seeing both sides of a connection. Start on the left, where Gateway Load Balancer uses a default five-tuple flow key with source and destination addresses, source and destination ports, and protocol. Supported three-tuple or two-tuple stickiness modes can serve other appliance requirements. The colored arrows show repeated packets in a selected flow reaching the same appliance. Next, follow the blue forward path and orange return path across the top-right panel. A stateful firewall may need both directions to traverse the appropriate inspection state. When integrating Transit Gateway or other routing components, validate symmetric routes and applicable appliance mode. In the lower-left, an appliance becomes unavailable. GWLB health checks can identify healthy replacement capacity, but the replacement appliance may not possess the original firewall session state. Existing traffic can therefore fail or need reconnection depending on configured failover behavior. Finish with the lower-right monitoring panel. Record throughput, appliance health, flow distribution, draining and real client experience during failures. Inspect not only whether a new appliance launches, but whether allowed sessions actually recover.
